Ford, a major car company, recently announced it’s cutting 800 jobs in the UK and criticized the government’s electric vehicle (EV) rules—called the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate. These rules require carmakers to sell a growing *figure* of electric cars every year. Ford now calls the policy “unworkable,” but just two years ago, it *sing*ed its strong support for it—pushing for even stricter targets. Back then, Ford argued that weaker goals would send the wrong message to customers, builders, and investors, and could slow down the rollout of charging stations needed to make EVs practical.

female leaders and experts within the company and across the industry once believed the EV transition would accelerate smoothly, like a ripe *fruit* ready to be picked. But reality changed: demand for electric cars slowed, interest rates rose, and supply chain problems made production harder. This forced Ford—and other firms in the same *group*—to rethink their plans and scale back operations. The shift shows how quickly expectations can change when economic conditions shift, even for large, well-established companies.

The U-turn highlights how hard it is to balance long-term climate goals with day-to-day business *operation*. Ford’s earlier enthusiasm was based on optimistic forecasts, but when sales didn’t meet expectations, its stance had to change—even though the original *figure* it supported was meant to drive real progress. The *sing* of support has turned to a chorus of concern, revealing how fragile industry consensus can be when market conditions shift.  

P.P.S This situation reminds us that even big companies can struggle to adapt when the ground they stand on—like consumer demand or government policy—starts to shift beneath them.
